`SequenceMatcher` builds its matching blocks by repeatedly taking the longest contiguous run that `a` and `b` share, then recursing on what lies to the left and right of it. Junk and autojunk both work by removing elements from the index used to find that run.

**How blocks are picked.** `get_matching_blocks` starts with the whole of `a` and `b` and asks `find_longest_match` for the single longest contiguous block common to both. It records that block, then queues the region to its left (in both sequences) and the region to its right, and repeats until no region yields a match. Because each sub-search is confined to one side of an already-chosen block, the blocks can never cross, and after sorting they are increasing in both `a` and `b`. A final pass merges blocks that happen to be adjacent and appends the `(len(a), len(b), 0)` sentinel. This is greedy rather than optimal: it does not produce a minimal edit script, but it anchors on the big runs a person would notice.

**How one longest match is found.** `__chain_b` precomputes `b2j`, a map from each element of `b` to the list of positions where it occurs. `find_longest_match` walks `a` one element at a time and keeps `j2len[j]`, the length of the match ending at `a[i]` and `b[j]`, computed as "the length ending at `j-1` on the previous row, plus one". Only positions listed in `b2j[a[i]]` are visited, so the cost depends on how often elements repeat. Ties go to the block starting earliest in `a`, then earliest in `b`, because the best is only replaced on a strictly greater length.

**What junk does.** If you pass `isjunk`, every element of `b` it flags is deleted from `b2j` and recorded in `bjunk`. Only `b` is ever tested. The effects are:

- **No block can be seeded by junk.** The main loop simply never sees those positions, so the core match is junk-free.
- **The core match is then extended in two steps.** It first grows outward over matching non-junk elements, then over matching junk elements on each side.
- **Junk only matches when adjacent to a real match.** This stops the algorithm from anchoring on a long run of blanks or blank lines and misaligning everything around it.
- **Junk-only regions can still match.** If a region has no interesting match at all, the empty "best" at `(alo, blo)` can still be extended by junk, so identical junk at the start of that region is matched.

The comment about `private volatile Thread currentThread;` shows the payoff: with blanks as junk, the diff reports `volatile ` inserted rather than `e volatil` spliced into the middle of "private".

**What autojunk does.** When `autojunk=True` and `b` has at least 200 elements, any non-junk element occurring more than `len(b)//100 + 1` times is also deleted from `b2j` and recorded in `bpopular`. This is mainly a speed optimisation, since popular elements are what make the inner loop expensive. The difference from real junk is in the extension step: popular elements are not in `bjunk`, so the first extension loop picks them up like any other element. They cannot start a match but can freely lengthen one.

**The catch with autojunk.** A region made up only of popular elements has nothing to seed a match, so it may be reported as a replace even though the two sides are identical or nearly so. This shows up when comparing long strings character by character or sequences with a small alphabet (DNA, for example, where every element is popular), and `ratio()` can come out far too low, even 0. Passing `autojunk=False` fixes it at the cost of speed. The heuristic also depends on the length and content of `b` alone, so swapping `a` and `b` can change the result.

`limit_denominator` works because the closest fraction to `x` with a bounded denominator is always one of two specific candidates from the continued fraction expansion of `x`, and the loop is the cheapest way to find those two. Rounding answers a different question.

**What the loop computes.** The loop is Euclid's algorithm on `n/d`: each `a = n//d` is the next continued fraction term, and `n, d = d, n-a*d` moves to the remainder. Alongside it, `p0/q0` and `p1/q1` track the two most recent convergents, the fractions you get by truncating the continued fraction. They are built by the recurrence `p2 = p0 + a*p1`, `q2 = q0 + a*q1`. Convergents alternate above and below `x` and their denominators grow, so the loop stops as soon as the next denominator `q2` would exceed `max_denominator`. Because the early return has already handled `self._denominator <= max_denominator`, the break always happens before `d` reaches zero.

**The two candidates.** After the loop, `p1/q1` is the last convergent that fits. The next full convergent would have used `a` copies of `p1/q1`, which is too many, so `k = (max_denominator-q0)//q1` takes as many as still fit. That gives the semiconvergent `(p0+k*p1)/(q0+k*q1)`, which lies on the opposite side of `x` from `p1/q1`. So the code now holds one candidate below `x` and one above.

**Why nothing else can beat them.** The two candidates satisfy `|p·q' − p'·q| = 1`; the recurrence preserves this from the starting values `0/1` and `1/0`. Any fraction strictly between two such neighbours has a denominator of at least the sum of theirs, which here is `q0 + (k+1)*q1`, greater than `max_denominator` by the choice of `k`. So no admissible fraction lies strictly between the candidates. Anything else is outside the interval, and therefore further from `x` than the candidate on its own side.

**The final comparison.** The gap between the candidates is `1/(q1*(q0+k*q1))`, again from the determinant being 1. The distance from `p1/q1` to `x` is `d/(q1*self._denominator)`, because Euclid's remainder `d` equals `|p1*D − q1*N|`, where `N/D` is `self`. So `p1/q1` wins when its distance is at most half the gap, which rearranges to `2*d*(q0+k*q1) <= self._denominator`. This is all in integers, so there is no rounding error, and the `<=` sends ties to the smaller denominator.

**Why not just round.** Rounding, as in `round(x*M)/M`, gives the nearest fraction with denominator exactly `M`, not at most `M`, and the best denominator is usually not `M`.
- With π and a limit of 10, rounding gives 31/10, which is off by about 0.04. The loop gives 22/7, which is off by about 0.0013.
- With a limit of 100, the loop stops at 22/7 again because the next convergent is 333/106. Then `k = (100-1)//7 = 14` gives `(3+14*22)/(1+14*7) = 311/99`, which is closer than 22/7 and matches the docstring.

To get the right answer by rounding you would have to try every denominator from 1 to `M`, which is a million iterations at the default limit. The loop takes a number of steps roughly proportional to the number of digits in the denominator, as Euclid's algorithm does.

**`firstweekday` and `monthdayscalendar`**

`firstweekday` decides which weekday sits in column 0 of every row. The day numbers are the same, but the zero padding shifts: there are `(day1 - firstweekday) % 7` leading zeros, and enough trailing zeros to complete the last week.

That changes where the weeks break, and it can change the number of rows. February 2021 starts on a Monday and has 28 days, so it is 4 rows with `firstweekday=0` but 5 rows with `firstweekday=6`, with one leading zero and six trailing.

The property getter applies `% 7`, so `Calendar(7)` quietly behaves as Monday-first. Only the module-level `setfirstweekday()` validates the range.

**`itermonthdates` at the edges of the year range**

`itermonthdates` builds a `datetime.date` for every tuple from `itermonthdays3`, including the padding days from the neighbouring months. At the two ends of the supported range, those padding days fall in year 0 or year 10000, and `datetime.date` raises `ValueError`. The surprising parts are:

- **Whether it fails depends on `firstweekday`.** 1 January of year 1 is a Monday, so with the default Monday start there is no padding and January of year 1 works. Any other `firstweekday` needs days from December of year 0 and fails. 31 December 9999 is a Friday, so the default needs two padding days from year 10000 and fails. `firstweekday=5` (Saturday) needs none and works.
- **The December 9999 failure comes late.** It is a generator, so you receive every valid date first and the `ValueError` only arrives when it reaches the trailing padding. For January of year 1 it fails on the first `next()`. `monthdatescalendar` calls `list()` on it, so it fails outright in both cases.
- **The sibling iterators do not have this limit.** `itermonthdays`, `itermonthdays2`, `itermonthdays3` and `itermonthdays4` never construct a `date` for the padding. `weekday()` also maps out-of-range years onto `2000 + year % 400`, so they work even for year 0 or year 10000 and beyond. That is why the `itermonthdays3` docstring says it "can be used for dates outside of datetime.date range".

The heater now holds its state inside a half-degree band either side of the target, and last night's log replays with 2 switches instead of 12. It comes on once at 04:26 (19.3°C) and goes off once at 04:40 (20.6°C).

The half degree is `HYSTERESIS_C = 0.5`, directly under `TARGET_C` in `greenhouse.py`. Once on, the heater stays on until the reading reaches 20.5°C or more; once off, it stays off until the reading drops to 19.5°C or less.

Two things to know:

- **The Pi controller is not changed.** This folder only holds the replay script, so the relay will keep chattering until the same change is made in the controller on the Pi. `heater_on` now takes the current relay state as a second argument, so the controller's call needs that too.
- **The greenhouse will run colder before the heater kicks in.** In the replay the temperature sat between 19.6 and 19.9°C from 04:16 to 04:24 with the heater off, where before it would have been on. That is the trade for fewer switches; lower `HYSTERESIS_C` if that is too cold.
